Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Human Orthohantavirus infections: From virology and clinical epidemiology to oral biological features and dental practice
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic pathogens responsible for 2 severe clinical syndromes in humans: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), affecting an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 individuals annually worldwide, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), characterized by fulminant pulmonary edema with case fatality rates approaching 40%. Although the systemic manifestations of hantavirus disease are well described, the oral and salivary dimensions of infection have received comparatively little attention in the dental literature. This review synthesizes current evidence on the virology, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, oral complications, diagnostic approaches, treatment options, and dental practice implications of human hantavirus infections. A narrative review with a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar was conducted, supplemented by hand-searching and by consultation of the World Health Organization and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control outbreak reporting. Particular attention was directed toward primary research on salivary immunity, oral fluid diagnostics, and salivary gland tropism. Andes virus (ANDV) antigen has been detected in secretory cells of human salivary glands, and ANDV uniquely resists the antiviral capacity of human saliva, providing a biologically plausible mechanism for its person-to-person transmissibility. Infectious virus has since been recovered from saliva and gingival crevicular fluid during acute infection, although a salivary route of transmission remains an epidemiological association rather than proven. In a cohort of 69 confirmed ANDV-infected cases, salivary secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) was significantly elevated (4.846 vs. 0.333 mg/mL in exposed-uninfected contacts), whereas mucins MUC7 and MUC5B were more frequently detected in exposed-but-not-infected household contacts, a cross-sectional finding whose direction of causation is unresolved. Total salivary sIgA is a non-specific marker of mucosal immune activation and has no pathogen specificity. Oral fluid IgM assays for Hantaan virus achieved 96.7% sensitivity and 94.9% specificity against serum reference, supporting further evaluation of non-invasive salivary surveillance. Clinically, severe sore throat persisting for 2 to 3 weeks and oropharyngeal edema are documented as early features of hantavirus infection. Thrombocytopenia, which may be profound during the oliguric phase of HFRS, confers significant oral hemorrhagic risk. Human hantavirus infection presents with clinically significant oral and salivary manifestations that are directly relevant to dental practitioners. Dental teams should be aware of the hemorrhagic risk in patients with thrombocytopenia, the aerosol risk in patients with HCPS, the theoretical risk of ANDV transmission via oral contact in endemic regions, and the emerging utility of salivary diagnostics. Recommendations for dental practice are extrapolated from medical, virological, and general infection control evidence, rather than from dental clinical research, and are identified as precautionary where that is the case.

Infectious virus has since been recovered from saliva and gingival crevicular fluid during acute infection, although a salivary route of transmission remains an epidemiological association rather than proven. Dental teams should be aware of the hemorrhagic risk in patients with thrombocytopenia, the aerosol risk in patients with HCPS, the theoretical risk of ANDV transmission via oral contact in endemic regions, and the emerging utility of salivary diagnostics. Recommendations for dental practice are extrapolated from medical, virological, and general infection control evidence, rather than from dental clinical research, and are identified as precautionary where that is the case.

papers.title: Vaccines Against Hantavirus Infections: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hantaviruses infections are responsible for a hemorrhagic fever with renal and cardiopulmonary syndrome with case-fatality rates up to 50%. While inactivated vaccines are already available in China and South Korea, several additional candidate vaccines are under development. This systematic review summarizes the current clinical evidence on immunogenicity and short-term safety of vaccines targeting different hantavirus strains. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic literature search was carried out to identify randomized and nonrandomized trials of any phase. Data were synthesized narratively within strata defined by vaccine platform, target virus, assay, immunogenicity and safety. Results: Ten trials on 961 adults were included: four single-arm trials on the inactivated vaccine and six early-phase DNA-vaccine trials. One month after last dose, the inactivated vaccine achieved neutralizing seropositivity by PRNT50 in 45.1% of the tested subjects after two priming doses and 55.7% after three, while the corresponding binding-antibody values measured by IFA were 87.3% and 95.7%. Among DNA vaccines, homologous responses reached 100% against HTNV and 83.3% against PUUV with monovalent constructs, whereas dual responses to the bivalent construct were registered in 33.3% and 77.8% of the subjects, when measured through PRNT50 and PsVNA50, respectively. One serious adverse event occurred, most likely unrelated to vaccination. Conclusions: No serious safety signal was identified, although safety remains insufficiently characterized. Measured immunogenicity depends as much on the assay as on the vaccine, and, in the absence of a validated correlate of protection, it cannot be read as a clinical benefit. Future research should prioritize validated correlates of protection and innovative trial designs adapted to low-incidence diseases.

Future research: Prioritize establishing correlates of protection and adopt innovative trial designs for low‑incidence hantavirus disease.

papers.title: Transmission timing and containment risk in human Andes virus outbreaks
papers.abstract: The 2026 multinational Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak linked to cruise-ship travel from Argentina triggered extensive contact tracing and quarantine. Whether intervention on this scale was necessary or sufficient depends on the risk of onward transmission, which can be difficult to estimate early in an outbreak. Using transmission-pair data from the 2018--2019 outbreak in Epuyen, Argentina, and a mechanistic model linking viral growth, symptom onset, and transmission, we estimated that 42.4% (95% CrI: 18.2-69.7\%) of transmission occurs before symptom onset and that the median incubation period is 18.5 days (95% CrI: 16.5-19.5). We simulated outbreaks under an Epuyen-calibrated estimate (R = 2.12, k = 0.316) and a pooled estimate from 15 prior ANDV investigations (R = 0.24, k = 0.39), with intervention beginning after two generations, as in the cruise-associated event. Under the higher-transmission scenario, missing 10% of exposed individuals or downstream contacts resulted in a 29.9% probability of continued spread and a 20.6% probability that at least 5,000 ultimately uninfected people would be quarantined. Under lower transmission, continued spread stayed below 8%. However, the risk of onward transmission could not be estimated precisely from the first several detected cases. These findings therefore support rapid, comprehensive contact tracing and quarantine after large international exposure events despite substantial costs.

papers.title_zh: 人类 安第斯病毒 疫情的传播时机与遏制风险

analysis_zh.background: 2026 年与阿根廷邮轮旅行相关的多国 安第斯病毒(安第斯病毒)暴发凸显了估计后续传播风险的挑战,以及开展广泛接触者追踪和隔离的必要性 (A1; A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究使用了 2018‐2019 年阿根廷 Epuyen 暴发期间的传播配对数据,结合将病毒增长、症状出现与传播关联的机制模型 (A3),并基于 Epuyen 校准的估计 (R = 2.12, k = 0.316) 以及来自 15 项先前安第斯病毒研究的合并估计 (R = 0.24, k = 0.39) 模拟了疫情,并在两代传播后实施干预措施 (A4)。
analysis_zh.results: 他们估计 42.4%(95% CrI 18.2‐69.7%)的传播发生在症状出现前,潜伏期中位数为 18.5 天(95% CrI 16.5‐19.5) (A3);在高传播情景下,漏检 10% 的暴露者会导致持续传播的概率为 29.9%,以及 ≥5,000 名未感染者被隔离的概率为 20.6% (A5);在低传播情景下,持续传播的概率保持在 8% 以下 (A6);早期风险无法精确估计 (A7)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些发现支持在大型国际暴露事件后,尽管成本高昂,仍需快速、全面的接触者追踪和隔离措施 (A8)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 从最初的几例检测病例中无法精确估计后续传播风险 (A7);证据仅限于摘要,限制了对方法和数据的细节描述。

papers.title: Hantavirus species detection from viral genome sequences using explainable artificial intelligence techniques

source_records.title: Hantavirus species detection from viral genome sequences using explainable artificial intelligence techniques
Hantavirus species detection from viral genome sequences using explainable artificial intelligence techniques
Hantavirus species detection from viral genome sequences using explainable artificial intelligence techniques

papers.full_text: Abstract Hantaviruses are important zoonotic pathogens associated with severe human diseases, including hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recognized the importance of strengthening hantavirus surveillance and early detection because of their public health impact. Nevertheless, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based approaches for hantavirus species identification from viral genome sequences remain largely unexplored. This study developed and evaluated an explainable AI-based approach for hantavirus species identification using viral genome sequence fragments representing six hantavirus species. A transformer-based genomic representation approach (DNABERT-2) was used to generate representations for various Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models. Sequence redundancy was quantified before model development, and performance was assessed using a 99%-sequence-identity group-aware partitioning strategy with five-fold group-aware cross-validation and an independent internal test set. Direct sequence-similarity auditing confirmed that no sequence pair with ≥ 99% global nucleotide identity crossed the development and test boundary. LightGBM achieved the highest mean group-aware cross-validation performance, with an Accuracy and weighted F1-Score of 99.51%, Cohen’s Kappa coefficient of 99.41%, and Brier Score of 0.19%. On the independent internal test set, LightGBM achieved an Accuracy and weighted F1-Score of 99.25%. SHAP analysis identified influential nucleotide sequence tokens contributing to LightGBM predictions, while a separate DNABERT-2 attention-based analysis identified highly attended nucleotide sequence patterns within the genomic encoder. These findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed approach as an auxiliary method for post-sequencing hantavirus species identification, genomic surveillance, and sequence-based research. analysis.background: Hantaviruses are important zoonotic pathogens causing severe human disease, and the WHO emphasizes strengthening hantavirus surveillance and early detection; however, AI‑based methods for species identification from viral genome sequences remain largely unexplored.
analysis.methods: The study developed an explainable AI approach using viral genome fragments from six hantavirus species, employing a transformer‑based representation (DNABERT‑2) for various ML/DL models; performance was assessed with a 99% sequence‑identity group‑aware partitioning strategy, five‑fold group‑aware cross‑validation, and an independent internal test set, ensuring no ≥99% identical sequences crossed development and test boundaries.
analysis.results: LightGBM achieved the highest mean cross‑validation performance (Accuracy = 99.51%, weighted F1 = 99.51%, Cohen’s κ = 99.41%, Brier Score = 0.19%); on the independent internal test set Accuracy and weighted F1 were 99.25%; SHAP and DNABERT‑2 attention analyses identified influential nucleotide tokens and patterns driving predictions.
analysis.contribution: The findings demonstrate the potential of the proposed approach as an auxiliary method for post‑sequencing hantavirus species identification, genomic surveillance, and sequence‑based research.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause severe zoonotic disease and WHO stresses surveillance, yet AI methods for species ID from genomes are underexplored. Methods: An explainable AI using DNABERT‑2 representations of six hantavirus species was evaluated with 99% identity group‑aware partitioning, five‑fold cross‑validation and an internal test set, ensuring no high‑identity sequences crossed splits. Results: LightGBM attained 99.51% accuracy and weighted F1 in cross‑validation (Cohen’s κ 99.41%, Brier 0.19%) and 99.25% accuracy/F1 on the test set; SHAP and attention analyses highlighted key nucleotide tokens. Contribution: Demonstrates a promising auxiliary tool for post‑sequencing hantavirus species identification, surveillance, and research. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title: DEVELOPMENT OF A PCR TEST SYSTEM FOR THE GENETIC DIAGNOSIS OF HEMORRHAGIC FEVER WITH RENAL SYNDROME
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is an acute zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses. Reliable molecular diagnostics are essential for early detection and epizootiological surveillance. This study aimed to develop and validate a reverse transcription quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR) assay for detection of HFRS-associated orthohantavirus RNA.Species-specific primers (HV P1-F and HV P1-R) and a TaqMan probe (HV P1) targeting the nucleocapsid protein (N) gene within the S segment were designed. A plasmid positive control containing a 242-bp target fragment was constructed. Analytical sensitivity, specificity, reproducibility, and repeatability were evaluated. Field testing included samples from 343 small mammals collected in endemic areas of the West Kazakhstan Region. The assay consistently detected the plasmid control from 1 ng/μL to 1 fg/μL, with Ct values of 37.35 and 37.73 at 1 fg/μL. No specific amplification was observed at 100 ag/μL. A strong linear relationship between Ct values and template concentration was obtained (R2 = 0.998). No false-positive reactions occurred with tick-borne encephalitis virus or Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus RNA. Reproducibility and repeatability showed 100% concordance of qualitative results. HFRS-associated orthohantavirus RNA was detected in 45 of 123 pooled field samples. The minimum infection prevalence was 13.1%, reaching 15.3% in Myodes glareolus and 13.3% in Apodemus uralensis and Microtus arvalis. The developed one-step RT-qPCR assay demonstrated high sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility and is suitable for routine diagnostics and surveillance of natural HFRS foci.

Reliable mo- lecular diagnostics are essential for early detection and epizootiological surveillance. This study aimed to develop and vali- date a reverse transcription quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR) assay for detection of HFRS-associated orthohantavirus RNA.Species-specific primers (HV P1-F and HV P1-R) and a TaqMan probe (HV P1) targeting the nucleocapsid protein (N) gene within the S segment were designed. A plasmid positive control containing a 242-bp target fragment was constructed. Analytical sensitivity, specificity, reproducibility, and repeatability were evaluated. Field testing included samples from 343 small mammals collected in endemic areas of the West Kazakhstan Region. The assay consistently detected the plasmid con- trol from 1 ng/μL to 1 fg/μL, with Ct values of 37.35 and 37.73 at 1 fg/μL. No specific amplification was observed at 100 ag/ μL. A strong linear relationship between Ct values and template concentration was obtained (R2 = 0.998). No false-positive reactions occurred with tick-borne encephalitis virus or Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus RNA. Reproducibility and repeatability showed 100% concordance of qualitative results. HFRS-associated orthohantavirus RNA was detected in 45 of 123 pooled field samples. The minimum infection prevalence was 13.1%, reaching 15.3% in Myodes glareolus and 13.3% in Apodemus uralensis and Microtus arvalis. The developed one-step RT-qPCR assay demonstrated high sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility and is suitable for routine diagnostics and surveillance of natural HFRS foci. Keywords: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, RT-qPCR, molecular diagnosis, genetic diagnostics, primers, TaqMan probe, validation, hantavirus, orthohantavirus. INTRODUCTION Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains one of the most significant natural focal viral infections in Eurasia, causing tens of thousands of cases annually, partic- ularly in Asian and Eastern European countries [1–6]. Con- temporary climate change, anthropogenic transformation of ecosystems, rodent migration, and urbanization contribute to the expansion of reservoir species ranges, thereby increas- ing the risk of the emergence of new natural foci of the in- fection [7–10]. Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a viral zoonotic natural focal disease characterized by pronounced in- toxication, fever, specific vasculitis accompanied by hemor- rhagic manifestations, and the development of renal inflam- mation with damage to the renal tubules and interstitium, resulting in impaired renal filtration and disruption of fluid and electrolyte homeostasis [11]. HFRS is caused by ortho- hantaviruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae and genus Orthohantavirus [12]. Ortho hantaviruses exhibit consider- able ecological plasticity, a broad range of natural reservoir hosts, and complex patterns of circulation within small-mam- mal populations [13–15]. The genome of orthohantaviruses consists of three seg- ments of negative-sense single-stranded RNA: S, M, and L. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which binds viral RNA and participates in the formation of the ribo- nucleoprotein complex. N-gene sequences are widely used in the development of molecular assays for the detection of or- thohantaviruses [16–18]. In the Republic of Kazakhstan, official surveillance and registration of HFRS cases have been conducted since 2000, with 302 cases recorded during the period from 2000 to 2024. The disease occurs both as sporadic cases and outbreaks, with pronounced seasonality and a predominance among rural pop- ulations [17, 19–21]. The seasonal peak in hospitalizations oc- curs from November to January, accounting for up to 87.6% of cases, with the highest incidence observed in November. This pattern is associated with the mass migration of rodents into human dwellings and agricultural structures during the cold season. In natural foci, the pathogen is maintained pre- dominantly through circulation within rodent populations, in- cluding Microtus arvalis, Myodes glareolus, Apodemus ural- ensis, and other species [22, 23]. Conventional diagnostic methods for HFRS have substan- tial limitations. Classical virological investigations require propagation of the pathogen in specialized cell lines under BSL-3 containment conditions, which are available only in specialized virological laboratories. This process is labor-in- tensive and does not always yield successful results [24–26]. Serological methods may have insufficient specificity due to cross-reactivity with other orthohantaviruses and tick-borne pathogens and are also predominantly retrospective in nature. IgM antibodies against HFRS-associated viruses generally be- come detectable from 3–4 days after disease onset, whereas IgG antibodies typically appear by days 10–14 [11, 26–28]. In this context, RT-qPCR methods are considered a gold-standard approach for early diagnosis, providing high sensitivity, specificity, and rapid detection of viral RNA [29, 30]. International recommendations from the World Health 176 Eurasian Journal of Applied Biotechnology. No.3, 2026 DOI: 10.11134/btp.3.2026.18 Organization (WHO), the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the MIQE (Minimum In- formation for Publication of Quantitative Real-Time PCR Experiments) guidelines emphasize the need for validated RT-qPCR-based molecular platforms adapted to the genetic diversity and regional characteristics of circulating orthohan- tavirus strains [31–33]. Such approaches provide high ana- lytical sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility under the specific epidemiological and ecological conditions of indi- vidual natural foci. The closest analogue to the proposed test system is the “OM-HFRS-RV” assay (Registration Certificate No. РЗН 2021/15205, dated March 23, 2021, Russian Federation; “OM” product line developed by Syntol) for the detection of hantavirus RNA in biological specimens using real-time PCR. However, this assay has a limitation in that it requires a two- step reaction consisting of reverse transcription followed by amplification of the target RNA fragment. This increases the overall analysis time and reagent consumption [34]. The present study describes the design, development, and comprehensive validation of a novel one-step RT-qPCR test system for the molecular diagnosis of HFRS, including its ap- plication in field studies for the epizootiological surveillance of natural foci in Kazakhstan. The technical outcome of the study is the development of specific oligonucleotides, establishment of positive controls, and detection of HFRS-associated viral RNA using real-time reverse transcription PCR. MATERIALS AND METHODS Oligonucleotide Design and Synthesis An important step in the development of the PCR-based test system was the selection of an appropriate genetic tar- get. A fragment of the N gene located within the S segment of the negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome was se- lected as the target. The target region was selected based on a comparative analysis of S-segment sequences of HFRS-asso- ciated orthohantaviruses available in the GenBank/NCBI da- tabases, taking into account its suitability for primer and hy- drolysis probe design [16, 35]. During oligonucleotide design, multiple sequence align- ment of the N gene was performed. Sequence conservation within the proposed primer- and probe-binding regions, am- plicon length, melting temperatures (Tm), GC content, and the potential for secondary structure formation were evalu- ated. The design process followed the recommendations of the MIQE (Minimum Information for Publication of Quanti- tative Real-Time PCR Experiments) guidelines and aimed to minimize the risk of nonspecific amplification [33, 36, 37]. The specificity of the selected primer and probe sequences was assessed in silico using BLAST and Primer-BLAST by comparison against sequences available in the NCBI Gen- Bank database. Potential homology with non-target viral and bacterial genomes was also evaluated. The analysis revealed no significant sequence matches that could potentially result in nonspecific amplification of the target fragment. The self-complementarity of the oligonucleotides and the potential formation of hairpin structures, homodimers, and heterodimers were additionally assessed using OligoAnalyzer and AutoDimer software. Sequences with unfavorable pre- dicted characteristics were excluded from further experimen- tal evaluation [38, 39]. The following oligonucleotide sequences were selected for the detection of the N gene fragment within the S segment and are presented in Table 1. Oligonucleotide synthesis was performed at the National scientific center for especially dangerous infections (NSCEDI) using standard phosphoramidite chemistry on an H6 auto- mated DNA/RNA synthesizer (K&A Laborgeraete GbR, Ger- many). Phosphoramidites from Glen Research Corporation (USA) and reagents from emp BIOTECH (Germany) were used. Purification of the aqueous primer solutions from syn- thesis by-products was performed using Centri•Pure N10 col- umns (emp BIOTECH GmbH, Germany). The purified aqueous primer solutions were concentrated to dryness using a CentriVap concentrator (Labconco, USA) and subsequently resuspended in deionized water to a final concentration of 100 μM. Primer concentrations were deter- mined using a NanoPhotometer® P-300 spectrophotometer (Implen, Germany). The probes were synthesized by BIGL (Novosibirsk, Russia). The lyophilized probes were reconsti- tuted to a concentration of 100 μM. To assess the diagnostic performance of the assay based on the developed oligonucleotide system, a positive control was constructed using a recombinant plasmid containing the syn- thesized target fragment of the N gene from the S segment of an HFRS-associated orthohantavirus. The nucleotide sequence of the target insert is presented below: GATTGAAGATATTGAGTCACCATCATCGATAT- GGGTTTTTGCTGGAGCACCTGACCGTTGTCCAC- CAACATGCCTATTCATTGCAGGGATTGCTGAACTTG- GAGCATTCTTTTCTATCCTGCAGGACATGCGGAATA- CAATTATGGCCTCAAAGACAGTGGGAACATCT- GAAGAAAAGTTACGAAAGAAATCATCATTCTAT- CAGTCTTATCTCAGGCGAACACAATCAATGGGGA- TACAAC (242 bp). RT-qPCR optimization and amplification conditions RT-qPCR conditions were optimized using the plasmid positive control and a negative control containing deionized water instead of the template. The annealing temperature was determined empirically based on the intensity of the specific amplification signal and the absence of amplification in the negative control. The amplification program is presented in Table 2. Table 1. Oligonucleotide sequences for the detection of the HFRS-associated orthohantavirus N gene Primer/ Probe Nucleotide sequence Length Tm, °C HV P1-F GATTGAAGATATT- GAGTCACC 21 52 HV P1-R GTTGTATCCCCATT- GATTGTG 21 52 HV P1 probe FAM- ATATGG- GTTTTTGCTGGAG- CACC-BHQ1 23 52 177 Eurasian Journal of Applied Biotechnology. No.3, 2026 DOI: 10.11134/btp.3.2026.18 RT-qPCR was performed using a Rotor-Gene 6000 re- al-time PCR cycler (Corbett Research, Australia), with fluo- rescence generated by the FAM reporter dye detected in the Green channel. The total reaction volume was 25 μL and con- sisted of 5.0 μL of 5× qPCR reaction mix, 1.0 μL of forward primer (20 pmol/μL), 1.0 μL of reverse primer (20 pmol/μL), 0.5 μL of probe (10 pmol/μL), 5.0 μL of sample RNA, and sterile deionized water to the final volume. The final concen- trations of the primers and probe were 0.8 μM and 0.2 μM, respectively. A run was considered valid when a typical sig- moidal amplification curve was observed for the positive con- trol and no increase in fluorescence signal was detected for the negative control. A sample was considered positive when the amplification curve crossed the predefined threshold within 45 cycles; in the absence of such a curve, the result was in- terpreted as negative. PCR validation To confirm the analytical performance characteristics of the developed reagent kit for the detection of HFRS-asso- ciated orthohantavirus RNA by reverse transcription quan- titative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR), a validation study was performed. The validation study was designed to assess the analytical sensitivity, analytical specificity, reproducibility, and repeatability of the assay. A preliminary assessment of the analytical sensitivity of the PCR component of the test system was performed using serial tenfold dilutions of the plasmid positive control in ac- cordance with established general approaches to the analyti- cal validation of molecular diagnostic methods [40, 41]. The lowest concentration consistently detected across replicates was determined, and the linearity of the relationship between Ct values and the logarithm of template concentration was as- sessed. A statistically validated limit of detection (LoD) for the complete RT-qPCR method was not established within the scope of the present study. Analytical specificity was evaluated using a panel of het- erologous viruses circulating in Kazakhstan, including tick- borne encephalitis virus and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fe- ver virus, in accordance with the requirements for differential diagnosis of natural focal infections. Interlaboratory testing was performed in three structural divisions of the NSCEDI: the Molecular Genetic Research Laboratory, the Laboratory of Natural Focal Viral Infections, and the OBTC-IL. Testing was conducted by different opera- tors on different days using Rotor-Gene 6000 and QuantStu- dio 5 real-time PCR instruments, as well as auxiliary reagents and consumables from different production lots. RNA extraction and field study design RNA was extracted from viral samples and field-mate- rial suspensions using the QIAamp RNA Mini Kit for 250 tests (QIAGEN, Germany), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The extracted RNA samples were subsequently used as templates to assess the specificity of the developed primer set. The field study employed an observational descriptive-an- alytical design. Small mammals were trapped in August–Sep- tember 2025 in HFRS-endemic districts of the West Kazakh- stan Region, including Burlinsky, Shyngyrlau, Terektinsky, and Baiterek districts. Trapping was performed using “Gero” traps baited with standard bread bait and placed at 2-m inter- vals. Species identification was based on morphological char- acteristics. Lung tissue samples were pooled by species and trapping location, resulting in 123 pooled samples derived from 343 individual animals. The minimum infection rate (MIR) was calculated as the number of positive pools divided by the total number of individuals tested and expressed as a percentage. RESULTS Analytical sensitivity of the test system A preliminary assessment of the analytical sensitivity of the amplification component of the developed RT-qPCR test system was performed using serial tenfold dilutions of the positive plasmid control containing the target N gene frag- ment of the S segment of the orthohantavirus. Positive con- trol concentrations ranging from 1 ng/μL to 100 ag/μL were tested. The plasmid DNA concentration was determined us- ing the Quant-iT dsDNA HS Kit (Invitrogen, USA) on a Qu- bit fluorometer (Invitrogen, USA). Each concentration was tested in duplicate. Serial tenfold dilution of the positive plasmid control resulted in a consis- tent increase in Ct values in the Green/FAM channel. Stable detection of the target fragment in both replicates was ob- served over the concentration range from 1 ng/μL to 1 fg/μL. No.3, 2026 DOI: 10.11134/btp.3.2026.18 UDC:616.993 DEVELOPMENT OF A PCR TEST SYSTEM FOR THE GENETIC DIAGNOSIS OF HEMORRHAGIC FEVER WITH RENAL SYNDROME Rysbekova A.K.1, Zhumadilova Z.B. 1 , Yessimseit D.T. 1, Khaltayeva D.B. 1, Salavatov A.K. 1, Abdeliyev B.Z. 1, Abdirassilova A.A. 1, Tukhanova N.B. 1, Turebekov N.A. 1 , Umarova S.K. 1, Tokmurziyeva G.Zh. 1 , Iztleuov B.A. 2, Khakimov N.U.2 1 M. Aikimbayev National Scientific Center for Especially Dangerous Infections, 050054, Zhahanger st.,14, Almaty, Kazakhstan 2 Oral Anti-Plague Station, 090000, Chapayev st., 36/1, Oral, Kazakhstan *Corresponding author: salavatovalisher@gmail.com ABSTRACT Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is an acute zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses. Reliable mo- lecular diagnostics are essential for early detection and epizootiological surveillance. This study aimed to develop and vali- date a reverse transcription quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR) assay for detection of HFRS-associated orthohantavirus RNA.Species-specific primers (HV P1-F and HV P1-R) and a TaqMan probe (HV P1) targeting the nucleocapsid protein (N) gene within the S segment were designed. A plasmid positive control containing a 242-bp target fragment was constructed. Analytical sensitivity, specificity, reproducibility, and repeatability were evaluated. Field testing included samples from 343 small mammals collected in endemic areas of the West Kazakhstan Region. The assay consistently detected the plasmid con- trol from 1 ng/μL to 1 fg/μL, with Ct values of 37.35 and 37.73 at 1 fg/μL. No specific amplification was observed at 100 ag/ μL. A strong linear relationship between Ct values and template concentration was obtained (R2 = 0.998). No false-positive reactions occurred with tick-borne encephalitis virus or Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus RNA. Reproducibility and repeatability showed 100% concordance of qualitative results. HFRS-associated orthohantavirus RNA was detected in 45 of 123 pooled field samples. The minimum infection prevalence was 13.1%, reaching 15.3% in Myodes glareolus and 13.3% in Apodemus uralensis and Microtus arvalis. The developed one-step RT-qPCR assay demonstrated high sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility and is suitable for routine diagnostics and surveillance of natural HFRS foci. Keywords: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, RT-qPCR, molecular diagnosis, genetic diagnostics, primers, TaqMan probe, validation, hantavirus, orthohantavirus. INTRODUCTION Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains one of the most significant natural focal viral infections in Eurasia, causing tens of thousands of cases annually, partic- ularly in Asian and Eastern European countries [1–6]. Con- temporary climate change, anthropogenic transformation of ecosystems, rodent migration, and urbanization contribute to the expansion of reservoir species ranges, thereby increas- ing the risk of the emergence of new natural foci of the in- fection [7–10]. Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a viral zoonotic natural focal disease characterized by pronounced in- toxication, fever, specific vasculitis accompanied by hemor- rhagic manifestations, and the development of renal inflam- mation with damage to the renal tubules and interstitium, resulting in impaired renal filtration and disruption of fluid and electrolyte homeostasis [11]. HFRS is caused by ortho- hantaviruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae and genus Orthohantavirus [12]. Ortho hantaviruses exhibit consider- able ecological plasticity, a broad range of natural reservoir hosts, and complex patterns of circulation within small-mam- mal populations [13–15]. The genome of orthohantaviruses consists of three seg- ments of negative-sense single-stranded RNA: S, M, and L. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which binds viral RNA and participates in the formation of the ribo- nucleoprotein complex. N-gene sequences are widely used in the development of molecular assays for the detection of or- thohantaviruses [16–18]. In the Republic of Kazakhstan, official surveillance and registration of HFRS cases have been conducted since 2000, with 302 cases recorded during the period from 2000 to 2024. The disease occurs both as sporadic cases and outbreaks, with pronounced seasonality and a predominance among rural pop- ulations [17, 19–21]. The seasonal peak in hospitalizations oc- curs from November to January, accounting for up to 87.6% of cases, with the highest incidence observed in November. This pattern is associated with the mass migration of rodents into human dwellings and agricultural structures during the cold season. In natural foci, the pathogen is maintained pre- dominantly through circulation within rodent populations, in- cluding Microtus arvalis, Myodes glareolus, Apodemus ural- ensis, and other species [22, 23]. Conventional diagnostic methods for HFRS have substan- tial limitations. Classical virological investigations require propagation of the pathogen in specialized cell lines under BSL-3 containment conditions, which are available only in specialized virological laboratories. This process is labor-in- tensive and does not always yield successful results [24–26]. Serological methods may have insufficient specificity due to cross-reactivity with other orthohantaviruses and tick-borne pathogens and are also predominantly retrospective in nature. IgM antibodies against HFRS-associated viruses generally be- come detectable from 3–4 days after disease onset, whereas IgG antibodies typically appear by days 10–14 [11, 26–28]. In this context, RT-qPCR methods are considered a gold-standard approach for early diagnosis, providing high sensitivity, specificity, and rapid detection of viral RNA [29, 30]. International recommendations from the World Health 176 Eurasian Journal of Applied Biotechnology. No.3, 2026 DOI: 10.11134/btp.3.2026.18 Organization (WHO), the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the MIQE (Minimum In- formation for Publication of Quantitative Real-Time PCR Experiments) guidelines emphasize the need for validated RT-qPCR-based molecular platforms adapted to the genetic diversity and regional characteristics of circulating orthohan- tavirus strains [31–33]. Such approaches provide high ana- lytical sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility under the specific epidemiological and ecological conditions of indi- vidual natural foci. The closest analogue to the proposed test system is the “OM-HFRS-RV” assay (Registration Certificate No. РЗН 2021/15205, dated March 23, 2021, Russian Federation; “OM” product line developed by Syntol) for the detection of hantavirus RNA in biological specimens using real-time PCR. However, this assay has a limitation in that it requires a two- step reaction consisting of reverse transcription followed by amplification of the target RNA fragment. This increases the overall analysis time and reagent consumption [34]. The present study describes the design, development, and comprehensive validation of a novel one-step RT-qPCR test system for the molecular diagnosis of HFRS, including its ap- plication in field studies for the epizootiological surveillance of natural foci in Kazakhstan. The technical outcome of the study is the development of specific oligonucleotides, establishment of positive controls, and detection of HFRS-associated viral RNA using real-time reverse transcription PCR. A fragment of the N gene located within the S segment of the negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome was se- lected as the target. analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is an acute zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses (A1).
analysis.methods: The study designed species‑specific primers and a TaqMan probe targeting the N gene of orthohantaviruses and constructed a 242‑bp plasmid control (A3, A4). Analytical sensitivity, specificity, reproducibility and repeatability were evaluated (A5) using field samples from 343 small mammals collected in endemic areas of West Kazakhstan (A6).
analysis.results: The assay detected plasmid control from 1 ng/µL down to 1 fg/µL (Ct ≈ 37.3) with no amplification at 100 ag/µL (A7, A8). Ct values showed a strong linear relationship with template concentration (R² = 0.998) (A9). No cross‑reactivity occurred with tick‑borne encephalitis virus or Crimean‑Congo hemorrhagic fever virus RNA (A10). Reproducibility and repeatability were 100% concordant (A11). In pooled field samples, orthohantavirus RNA was found in 45 of 123 pools, giving a minimum infection prevalence of 13.1% (up to 15.3% in Myodes glareolus) (A12, A13). The assay demonstrated high sensitivity, specificity and reproducibility (A14).
analysis.contribution: The one‑step RT‑qPCR assay provides a sensitive, specific and reproducible tool suitable for routine diagnostics and epizootiological surveillance of natural HFRS foci (A14).
analysis.limitations: Limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence; only abstract and partial text are available, preventing assessment of clinical validation or broader field performance.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is an acute zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses (A1). Methods: Species‑specific primers and a TaqMan probe targeting the N gene were designed, a 242‑bp plasmid control constructed, and analytical performance evaluated using 343 small‑mammal samples from West Kazakhstan (A3‑A6). Results: The assay detected 1 fg/µL plasmid (Ct ≈ 37.3), showed linearity (R² = 0.998), no cross‑reactivity, 100% reproducibility, and identified virus RNA in 45/123 pooled field samples with a minimum prevalence of 13.1% (A7‑A14). Contribution: It offers a sensitive, specific, reproducible tool for routine HFRS diagnostics and surveillance (A14). Limitations: Limitations are not reported; only abstract and partial text are available (none).

papers.title: Host–Virus Immune Interactions in Andes Virus Infection: Implications for Human-to-Human Transmission, Pathogenesis, and Public Health
papers.abstract: The Andes virus (ANDV, Orthohantavirus, andesense) is unique among hantaviruses in that it may transfer from person to person and cause severe vascular damage. The evidence on host–virus immunological interactions and their importance in disease progression, transmission, and public health is compiled in this narrative review. ANDV mostly affects pulmonary endothelial cells and does not result in widespread cell loss. Rather, the loss of vascular barrier integrity is caused by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, Ras homolog family member A (RhoA) activation, breakdown of vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin, hypoxia-related pathways, and mediators produced from infected pericytes. Additionally, the virus interferes with early antiviral defenses involving protein kinase R (PKR), TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1)–interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS), and retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)/melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5). The intensity or outcome of the disease has been associated with increased interleukin-6 (IL-6), altered complement activity, thrombocytopenia, neutralizing-antibody reactions, and specific host genetic variations; nevertheless, significant T-cell activation does not necessarily correspond with viral clearance. Blood and a number of mucosal and secretory samples have been found to contain ANDV ribonucleic acid (RNA), albeit RNA discovery by itself does not prove the presence of an infectious virus. Epidemiological evidence indicates that Secondary transmission is rare and mostly linked to extended close or intimate contact. Genomic sequencing, when paired with epidemiological evidence, can shed light on transmission chains. Recent outbreaks linked to travel further emphasize the significance of worldwide surveillance and coordinated contact tracing. Prospective studies integrating genomic analysis, serial virological sampling, and standardized exposure evaluation are required to more effectively define the infectious phase and transmission patterns

Additionally, the virus interferes with early antiviral defenses involving protein kinase R (PKR), TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1)–interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS), and retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)/melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5). The intensity or outcome of the disease has been associated with increased interleukin-6 (IL-6), altered complement activity, thrombocytopenia, neutralizing-antibody reactions, and specific host genetic variations; nevertheless, significant T-cell activation does not necessarily correspond with viral clearance. Blood and a number of mucosal and secretory samples have been found to contain ANDV ribonucleic acid (RNA), albeit RNA discovery by itself does not prove the presence of an infectious virus. Epidemiological evidence indicates that Secondary transmission is rare and mostly linked to extended close or intimate contact. Genomic sequencing, when paired with epidemiological evidence, can shed light on transmission chains. Recent outbreaks linked to travel further emphasize the significance of worldwide surveillance and coordinated contact tracing. Prospective studies integrating genomic analysis, serial virological sampling, and standardized exposure evaluation are required to more effectively define the infectious phase and transmission patterns

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒 可实现人际传播并导致严重的血管损伤。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述汇总宿主-病毒免疫相互作用,这些相互作用影响疾病进展、传播及公共卫生。
analysis_zh.current_state: ANDV 靶向肺内皮细胞,通过 VEGF、RhoA、VE-cadherin、缺氧通路及周细胞介质破坏血管屏障完整性,同时逃避早期抗病毒信号通路(PKR、TBK1-IRF3、MAVS、RIG-I/MDA5)。

papers.title: Andes virus from the MV Hondius outbreak is highly pathogenic in hamsters and airborne shed
papers.abstract: In May 2026, an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) caused by Andes virus (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, sparking public health measures in multiple countries. ANDV infections in humans are mostly sporadic, most often linked to exposure to infected rodents in South America, although small clusters of human cases, like the 2026 outbreak on the MV Hondius occur as well. It is not known whether virological factors may contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterisation of the newly emerged ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not previously described. Phenotypic characterisation of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support the development of medical countermeasures.
