Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus 39 through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages 40 housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived 41 ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These 42 findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not 43 previously described. Phenotypic characterization of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal 44 models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support 45 the development of medical countermeasures. 46 3 | P a g e INTRODUCTION 47 On the 2nd of May 2026, a cluster of severe respiratory disease aboard the Dutch cruise ship MV 48 Hondius was notified to the World Health organization (WHO)1-3. Soon after, ANDV was 49 diagnosed as the cause of the outbreak, which overall led to 13 reported cases, including three 50 deaths4. Confirmed cases were all aboard the MV Hondius, although the outbreak led to 51 monitoring of 653 individuals in 33 countries around the globe. 52 ANDV is classified within the family Orthohantaviridae5-8. These are viruses that cause two distinct 53 disease complexes: the hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Europe and Asia, and 54 the hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, caused among others by Sin Nombre 55 virus (SNV) and Andes virus (ANDV), respectively9. HPS is usually presents in four distinct clinical 56 phases: febrile, cardiopulmonary, diuretic and convalescent10,11. Most cases are characterized by 57 pulmonary edema driven by increased vascular permeability, terminally leading to cardiogenic 58 shock and death12. The case fatality rate of the MV Hondius outbreak was 23%, lower than for 59 previously reported ANDV clusters. Direct comparison is difficult however, due to the relatively 60 low number of cases in this outbreak and early access to medical care for many of the individuals 61 affected13-15. 62 ANDV is endemic in Southern Argentina and Chile, where it causes seasonal outbreaks every 63 year9,16. Humans are believed to become infected mostly after exposure to aerosolized infectious 64 excretions of the rodent reservoir, the long-tailed rice rat (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus)5,6,17. 65 Andes virus (ANDV) was first detected in 1995, when it caused an outbreak of 16 cases and nine 66 deaths18. This outbreak and subsequent ones suggested that ANDV can be capable of human- 67 to-human transmission, with the main risk factor being in close contact with infected individuals in 68 enclosed settings18,19. Some cases have also been described without any documented direct 69 contact, hinting at a respiratory transmission route, though available data cannot distinguish 70 airborne shedding of infectious virus from contamination of the surrounding environment20. On 71 the MV Hondius, patients were in direct contact with each other, suggesting ANDV human-to- 72 4 | P a g e human transmission. One potential asymptomatic case of ANDV infection in a health-care worker 73 with low-level viraemia was also reported, despite only indirect exposure21-23. 74 Few studies have phenotyped ANDV isolates obtained directly from human patients21-23, and 75 fewer still have done so in vivo to define key viral characteristics such as virulence and host 76 responses22,24. This reflects the sporadic nature of HPS and its restricted geographical distribution. 77 ANDV is also notoriously difficult to isolate, as infection is typically diagnosed once patients have 78 already developed neutralizing antibodies. As a result, our understanding of the biological 79 differences between ANDV isolates associated with different cases and outbreaks is incomplete. 80 Here, we characterized the ANDV isolate associated with the MV Hondius outbreak 81 (ANDV/2026/hondius-NL-12, henceforth ANDV2026). Using the golden Syrian hamster model, we 82 studied viral pathogenesis, replication sites, and the host innate and adaptive immune responses. 83 We also analyzed virus shedding from infected animals and sampled air from the cages of infected 84 hamsters for ANDV RNA and infectious virus. Throughout our study, the human isolate ANDV2026 85 was compared with a rodent-derived ANDV strain (ANDV9717869). Altogether, in vivo phenotyping 86 contributes to the continuous risk assessment of emerging viruses of global health concern. 87 88 RESULTS 89 90 ANDV2026 causes severe, systemic infection in hamsters. Golden Syrian hamsters were 91 intranasally inoculated with a low dose (200 TCID50/hamster) of either ANDV2026 (n=18) or 92 ANDV9717869 (n=18). ANDV2026 was isolated from whole-blood sample collected from a pre- 93 symptomatic patient during the 2026 ANDV outbreak linked to the cruise ship MV Hondius3. 94 Backtitration of the inocula revealed that the animals received a dose of 28 TCID50 of ANDV2026 95 and 89 TCID50 of ANDV9717869. Six animals per group were sacrificed at 3, 7 and 14 days post- 96 inoculation (dpi), or earlier when reaching humane endpoints. Sixty percent of the hamsters 97 inoculated with ANDV2026 reached the humane endpoint between 12 and 14 dpi (Fig 1a). 98 5 | P a g e Symptoms included lethargy, ruffled fur, decreased mobility, and severe respiratory distress. In 99 general, animals reached humane endpoints within 24-72 hours after the onset of symptoms. The 100 development of clinical symptoms was also accompanied by a loss of body weight of up to 9% in 101 three days (Fig. 1b). At the terminal stage of the experiment (12-14 dpi), the lung-to-bodyweight 102 ratio of ANDV2026 inoculated animals was significantly increased when compared to both mock- 103 and ANDV9717869-inoculated animals (Fig. 1c). These values reflected the macroscopic lung 104 lesions observed in ANDV2026 inoculated animals, characterized by increased size, rounded edges 105 and darkened color with severe, diffuse lung oedema (Fig. 1d), as described previously for severe 106 ANDV infections in hamsters25-27. 107 Next, we tested 15 respiratory and non-respiratory tissues for presence of both viral RNA by qRT- 108 PCR and infectious virus by titration (Fig. 1e,f). At the early timepoints (3 dpi), viral RNA and 109 infectious virus were only detected in the nasal turbinates with titers essentially identical in both 110 ANDV2026- and ANDV9717869-inoculated animals. At 7 and 12-14 dpi all tissues contained both viral 111 RNA and infectious virus with titers in most cases higher in ANDV2026-infected animals. 112 Interestingly, we observed no significant differences in viral loads in myocardium and liver 113 between ANDV2026- and ANDV9717869-infected hamsters 12-14 dpi. These tissues were previously 114 reported as the prime targets of virus replication in ANDV9717869-infected hamsters26. We observed 115 the highest viral titers in the respiratory tract (nasal turbinates and lungs), submandibular salivary 116 glands, pancreas, and adrenal glands collected from ANDV2026-infected animals. 117 Sites of ANDV replication. Next, we investigated the sites of viral replication using 118 immunohistochemistry (IHC) and RNA in situ-hybridisation (ISH) in formalin-fixed and paraffin 119 embedded samples from inoculated animals. In the lungs, we detected abundant viral RNA (Fig. 120 2a) and protein in ANDV2026-infected animals at 7dpi, with widespread distribution in the 121 parenchyma. Quantification of RNA signal showed virus spread in wider areas of the lungs in 122 ANDV2026-infected hamsters compared to those infected with ANDV9717869 (Fig. 2b-c), both at 7 123 and 14 dpi. Virus RNA was detectable, both by qualitative assessment of the histological sections 124 6 | P a g e and by software-assisted image analysis28, in the lung parenchyma and endothelial cells, but not 125 in the bronchial epithelium of all ANDV infected animals at both 7 and 14 dpi (Fig. 2c-d). As 126 expected, extrarespiratory organs such as liver, kidney, myocardium, and many others showed 127 abundant viral RNA signal in endothelial cells, while epithelial cells were viral RNA negative (Fig. 128 2e). Importantly, we also detected ANDV2026 widely distributed in the brain, including in endothelial 129 cells of blood vessels, meninges and neurons (Fig. 2e and Fig. S1). 130 The widespread infection of endothelial cells throughout all organs was not accompanied by 131 severe histopathological lesions in both groups of animals. Serum chemistry revealed reduced 132 total protein and albumin concentrations in ANDV2026-infected hamsters compared to ANDV9717869- 133 and mock-infected animals, consistent with endothelial dysfunction and leakage of proteins to the 134 extravascular space (Fig. 2f). We found moderately abnormal values for alkaline phosphatase, 135 alanine-aminotransferase, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine and phosphorus in ANDV2026-infected 136 animals (in the terminal stages of the disease), consistent with kidney and liver damage, although 137 major histopathological lesions were not observed (Fig. 2f, Fig. S2). Serum values of amylase, 138 calcium, glucose, sodium and total bilirubin remained similar between groups (Fig. S2). 139 Lung pathology in ANDV2026-infected hamsters correlates with preferential activation of the 140 type I IFN response. At the latest stages of disease, we detected histopathological lesions 141 throughout the lungs in hamsters infected with ANDV2026, similar to severe HPS previously 142 described in this model 25-27. Lesions include diffuse alveolar damage, multifocal, 143 lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, alveolar histiocytosis, alveolar oedema, leukocytolastic vasculitis, 144 perivascular oedema, sloughing of bronchial epithelial cells to various degrees and hemorrhages 145 in the vessel (Fig. 3a-b). We also detected fibrin accumulation in damaged alveoli in more severe 146 cases (Fig. 3b, middle panel). Infiltrates of both B-cells (Pax+ cells) and macrophage (Iba-1+ cells) 147 infiltrates, but not T-cells (CD3+), were observed in the lungs of ANDV2026-infected animals (Fig. 148 3c-d). 149 7 | P a g e In addition, activation of the type I IFN response (henceforth IFN), assessed by the upregulation 150 of the IFN-stimulated gene Mx-1, was evident in the lungs of both ANDV2026- and ANDV9217869- 151 infected animals (Fig. 3d, last column). We detected relatively little Mx-1 at 7 dpi despite the 152 presence of abundant virus replication. This observation reinforces the concept that ANDV is able 153 to evade recognition by the host IFN response for some time. 154 Because ANDV, both in humans and in hamsters, causes primarily a pulmonary disease, we 155 further investigated whether the levels of the IFN response vary between lungs and other organs 156 (Fig. 4). To this end, we quantified the expression of IFIT-1 RNA, another interferon stimulated 157 gene (ISG), in FFPE sections of lungs, spleen, myocardium, kidney and liver of ANDV2026-infected 158 animals by RNAscope and normalized the data in relation to the presence of viral RNA in each of 159 these organs. We found the highest relative expression of IFIT-1 RNA in the lungs, followed by 160 the spleen (Fig. 4). These data are in line with the relatively upregulation of proinflammatory 161 genes such as CXCL10 that we detected in these two organs (Fig. S3). Of note, we did find 162 bronchial epithelial cells expressing ISGs in the absence of viral replication (Fig. 4a), most likely 163 triggered by an IFN response in infected neighboring cells. The IFN and inflammatory response 164 in respiratory epithelia may explain the lesions (sloughed off cells) observed in some of these 165 animals. 166 Combined, ANDV2026 causes a disease comparable to HPS in hamsters, characterized 167 predominantly by lung pathology, endothelial cell dysfunction, with a relatively long incubation 168 period where abundant virus replication does not trigger a detectable inflammatory response. 169 Adaptive immune response to ANDV in experimentally inoculated hamsters. We next 170 assessed antibody and T-cell responses in ANDV-infected animals. We detected neutralizing 171 antibodies only at 12-14 dpi in sera from animals infected with either ANDV9717869 or ANDV2026. 172 The mean VNT50 did not differ significantly between groups, even though all ANDV2026-infected 173 animals mounted a response compared to 40% of the ANDV9717689-infected animals (Fig. 5a). To 174 further characterize the ANDV-specific adaptive immune response, we isolated lymphocytes from 175 8 | P a g e hamster lungs at both 7 and 14 dpi and stimulated them with overlapping peptide pools covering 176 the N, Gn, Gc, and L proteins (the latter split in four distinct pools, L1-4) (Fig. 5b). At 7 dpi, antigen- 177 specific T-cell responses were limited in all groups (Fig. 5d). However, strong antigen-specific T- 178 cell responses were detected at 12-14 dpi regardless of group. The majority of virus-specific T- 179 cells targeted the L-protein (Fig. 5c, Fig. S4); these were comparable between ANDV9717869- and 180 ANDV2026-inoculated hamsters, and higher than those observed in mock-inoculated animals, 181 although significance was reached only for ANDV9717869 (Fig. 5e). N-specific T-cell responses 182 were higher in ANDV9717869-inoculated animals than in ANDV2026- and mock-inoculated animals at 183 12-14 dpi (Fig. 5e). Similar responses were observed with lymphocytes isolated from the spleen, 184 although the background in mock-inoculated hamsters was higher, complicating data 185 interpretation (Fig. S4). 186 Infectious virus is shed in the air by ANDV2026-infected animals. The ANDV outbreak aboard 187 the MV Hondius raised questions about the potential of increased shedding, and hence increased 188 transmissibility, of ANDV. In hamsters, we detected viral genomes (Fig. 6a) and infectious virus 189 (Fig. S5) in throat swabs of all ANDV2026-inoculated animals from 7 dpi onwards, with 190 progressively increasing titers until the end of the experiment (Fig. 6a). We detected infectious 191 virus in only one ANDV9717869-infected animal. By immunohistochemistry, we detected numerous 192 clusters of ANDV2026 infected endothelial cells, olfactory epithelium, degenerated and sloughing 193 olfactory epithelium, as well as the ducts of the nasal submucosal glands of the olfactory portion 194 of the turbinates, especially at 14 dpi. Only very few cells of the respiratory epithelium showed 195 occasionally virus positive signal (Fig. 6d-f). ANDV9717869-inoculated animals displayed only 196 occasional virus-positive cells in the nasal turbinates (either endothelial cells, cells within the 197 olfactory epithelium, or the submucosal glands). 198 We also detected ANDV2026 RNA in urine collected at study endpoints, but volumes were too small 199 to test for presence of infectious virus. Furthermore, we detected both viral RNA and infectious 200 9 | P a g e virus in feces homogenates collected from cages housing ANDV2026 infected animals (Fig. 6c and 201 S5). 202 Hence, ANDV2026-infected animals shed infectious virus from the respirat…

Wilbrink1#, Vanessa Herder1#, Kim Handrejk1#, Fabien Filaire1#, 4 Georgios Ilia2, Wai Wai Jones2, Luca M. Zaeck1, Debby van Eck Schipper1, Vincent P. Vaes1, 5 Sandhya Shrestha3, Johan Reimerink3, Laura L.A. van Dijk1, Mark Power1, Merel R. te Marvelde1, 6 Dennis de Meulder1, Hayley Cassidy1, Koen Wijnans1, Sharona Sacharoen–Rugebregt1, Alba 7 Grifoni4, Alessandro Sette4,5, Bas B. Oude Munink1, Chantal B.E.M. Reusken3,6, Bart L. 8 Haagmans1*, Rory D. de Vries1*, Sander Herfst1,7*, Massimo Palmarini 1,2* 9 10 1Department of Viroscience, Erasmus University Medical Center, Rotterdam, the Netherlands 11 2MRC-University of Glasgow Center for Virus Research, Glasgow, Scotland, United Kingdom 12 3Centre for Infectious Disease Control, National Institute for Public Health and the Environment 13 (RIVM), Bilthoven, the Netherlands. 14 4La Jolla Institute for Immunology, La Jolla, CA, USA 15 5Department of Medicine, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA 16 6Virology group, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Utrecht University, Utrecht, The Netherlands 17 7Pandemic and Disaster Preparedness Center, Delft, Rotterdam, The Netherlands. 18 19 #These authors contributed equally to this manuscript 20 *These senior authors contributed equally to this manuscript 21 Correspondence: m.palmarini@erasmusmc.nl 22 23 2 | P a g e Summary 24 In May 2026, an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) caused by Andes virus 25 (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, sparking public health measures in 26 multiple countries. ANDV infections in humans are mostly sporadic, most often linked to exposure 27 to infected rodents in South America, although small clusters of human cases, like the 2026 28 outbreak on the MV Hondius occur as well. It is not known whether virological factors may 29 contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterization of the newly emerged 30 ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a 31 presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral 32 replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in 33 golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe 34 pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and 35 inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we 36 detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. 37 Infected animals mounted neutralizing antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed 38 predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus 39 through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages 40 housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived 41 ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These 42 findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not 43 previously described. Phenotypic characterization of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal 44 models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support 45 the development of medical countermeasures. 46 3 | P a g e INTRODUCTION 47 On the 2nd of May 2026, a cluster of severe respiratory disease aboard the Dutch cruise ship MV 48 Hondius was notified to the World Health organization (WHO)1-3. Soon after, ANDV was 49 diagnosed as the cause of the outbreak, which overall led to 13 reported cases, including three 50 deaths4. Confirmed cases were all aboard the MV Hondius, although the outbreak led to 51 monitoring of 653 individuals in 33 countries around the globe. 52 ANDV is classified within the family Orthohantaviridae5-8. These are viruses that cause two distinct 53 disease complexes: the hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Europe and Asia, and 54 the hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, caused among others by Sin Nombre 55 virus (SNV) and Andes virus (ANDV), respectively9. HPS is usually presents in four distinct clinical 56 phases: febrile, cardiopulmonary, diuretic and convalescent10,11. Most cases are characterized by 57 pulmonary edema driven by increased vascular permeability, terminally leading to cardiogenic 58 shock and death12. The case fatality rate of the MV Hondius outbreak was 23%, lower than for 59 previously reported ANDV clusters. Direct comparison is difficult however, due to the relatively 60 low number of cases in this outbreak and early access to medical care for many of the individuals 61 affected13-15. 62 ANDV is endemic in Southern Argentina and Chile, where it causes seasonal outbreaks every 63 year9,16. Humans are believed to become infected mostly after exposure to aerosolized infectious 64 excretions of the rodent reservoir, the long-tailed rice rat (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus)5,6,17. 65 Andes virus (ANDV) was first detected in 1995, when it caused an outbreak of 16 cases and nine 66 deaths18. This outbreak and subsequent ones suggested that ANDV can be capable of human- 67 to-human transmission, with the main risk factor being in close contact with infected individuals in 68 enclosed settings18,19. Some cases have also been described without any documented direct 69 contact, hinting at a respiratory transmission route, though available data cannot distinguish 70 airborne shedding of infectious virus from contamination of the surrounding environment20. On 71 the MV Hondius, patients were in direct contact with each other, suggesting ANDV human-to- 72 4 | P a g e human transmission. One potential asymptomatic case of ANDV infection in a health-care worker 73 with low-level viraemia was also reported, despite only indirect exposure21-23. 74 Few studies have phenotyped ANDV isolates obtained directly from human patients21-23, and 75 fewer still have done so in vivo to define key viral characteristics such as virulence and host 76 responses22,24. This reflects the sporadic nature of HPS and its restricted geographical distribution. 77 ANDV is also notoriously difficult to isolate, as infection is typically diagnosed once patients have 78 already developed neutralizing antibodies. As a result, our understanding of the biological 79 differences between ANDV isolates associated with different cases and outbreaks is incomplete. 80 Here, we characterized the ANDV isolate associated with the MV Hondius outbreak 81 (ANDV/2026/hondius-NL-12, henceforth ANDV2026). Using the golden Syrian hamster model, we 82 studied viral pathogenesis, replication sites, and the host innate and adaptive immune responses. 83 We also analyzed virus shedding from infected animals and sampled air from the cages of infected 84 hamsters for ANDV RNA and infectious virus. Throughout our study, the human isolate ANDV2026 85 was compared with a rodent-derived ANDV strain (ANDV9717869). Altogether, in vivo phenotyping 86 contributes to the continuous risk assessment of emerging viruses of global health concern. 87 88 RESULTS 89 90 ANDV2026 causes severe, systemic infection in hamsters. Golden Syrian hamsters were 91 intranasally inoculated with a low dose (200 TCID50/hamster) of either ANDV2026 (n=18) or 92 ANDV9717869 (n=18). analysis.summary_en: Background: An outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome caused by Andes virus (ANDV) aboard the MV Hondius in May 2026 underscored the need to investigate virological factors influencing such clusters. Methods: Researchers isolated ANDV from a presymptomatic patient and infected golden Syrian hamsters, comparing the new ANDV2026 strain to a rodent‑derived ANDV9717869 control, assessing viral replication sites, immune responses, and shedding via air samplers. Results: ANDV2026 proved highly pathogenic, inducing severe pulmonary disease, delayed type‑I IFN and inflammatory responses, and replication in respiratory and extra‑respiratory tissues including brain; infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T‑cell responses against L and N proteins; multiple shedding routes were observed with infectious virus detected in air samples, whereas the control strain shed little virus and air samples were negative. Contribution: The findings consolidate established ANDV pathogenesis features while revealing novel properties such as airborne shedding, strengthening outbreak preparedness, identifying severity markers, and supporting countermeasure development. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒 来自 MV Hondius 爆发的病毒在仓鼠中高度致病并通过空气排出

analysis_zh.background: 2026年5月,在邮轮 MV Hondius 上检测到由 安第斯病毒(安第斯病毒)引起的 汉坦病毒肺综合征(汉坦病毒肺综合征)暴发,凸显了了解可能影响此类聚集的病毒学因素的必要性。
analysis_zh.methods: 研究人员从一名无症状患者中分离出安第斯病毒,并感染金叙利亚仓鼠,将新株 ANDV2026 与啮齿动物来源的 ANDV9717869 对照株进行比较;他们检查了病毒复制部位、先天性和适应性免疫反应,并通过空气采样器定量病毒脱落。
analysis_zh.results: ANDV2026 在仓鼠中高度致病,导致严重肺部疾病、I型干扰素和炎症反应延迟,以及在呼吸系统及包括脑在内的非呼吸组织中复制;感染动物产生针对 L 蛋白和 N 蛋白的中和抗体和 T 细胞反应;观察到多种脱落途径,空气样本检测到有感染性病毒,而对照株的脱落量很少,空气样本为阴性。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究整合了已知的安第斯病毒致病特征,同时揭示了如空气脱落等新特性,从而加强疫情防备,识别重症标志物,并支持医学对策的研发。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告。

papers.title: Design and in silico evaluation of PV-GNProtecta: an mRNA multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Puumala virus using immunoinformatics and structural analysis.
papers.abstract: Abstract Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population coverage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escherichia coli -based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection.

source_records.abstract: Abstract Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population coverage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escherichia coli -based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection.

Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s44342-026-00081-8. Introduction Nephropathia epidemica (NE) is attributed to Puumala virus (PUUV), a naturally occurring form of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in humans, which is a zoonotic infectious disease and generally considered a mild-to-moderate form of hantavirus infection within the HFRS spectrum. PUUV (Puumala orthohantavirus) is classified within the genus Orthohantavirus, family Hantaviridae, and order Bunyavirales, as defined by current ICTV taxonomy, and it was previously grouped under the family Bunyaviridae prior to taxonomic reclassification. PUUV infection presents with highly variable outcomes, ranging from subclinical cases (70–80%) to severe HFRS, and carries a fatality rate of about 0.1%. PUUV infection commonly presents with sudden fever, headache, back pain, nausea, gastrointestinal symptoms, thrombocytopenia, hematuria, and varying degrees of acute kidney impairment. In some patients, additional manifestations such as blurred vision, dizziness, insomnia, respiratory complications, oliguria, and subsequent polyuria during recovery may also occur. Although PUUV infection is generally considered mild, severe complications can occur in a subset of patients, including acute kidney failure, hypotension, shock, pulmonary edema, Guillain-Barré syndrome, respiratory distress, disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC), myocarditis, encephalitis, pituitary hemorrhage, seizures, and, in rare cases, multiorgan failure or fatal cerebral hemorrhage. The first identification of PUUV occurred in the early 1980s when the virus was isolated from bank voles (Myodes glareolus) in the Puumala region of Finland. Between July 1989 and June 1996, Finland reported 6701 PUUV infection cases confirmed via serological assays, with the highest incidence in the Itä-Savo district and a mortality rate below 0.1%, and later from 1995 to 2008, 22,681 cases were recorded with an average annual incidence of 31 per 100,000 population, resulting in 13 deaths and 52% of patients requiring hospitalization. PUUV accounts for approximately 93% of all notified hantavirus infections in Germany and caused a major outbreak in 2007 in Baden-Württemberg with 1089 reported human cases, while the highest annual number of PUUV infections in Germany was recorded in 2010 since hantavirus surveillance began in 2001. Also in 2007, Sweden’s Västerbotten County experienced a surprisingly severe outbreak of PUUV infection, with NE rates hitting 313 cases per 100,000 residents. Between 2001 and 2017, a total of 12,148 hantavirus disease cases were recorded, of which 9714 (approximately 97.41%) were attributed to PUUV infection. In 2019, Europe recorded over 4000 hantavirus cases (0.8 per 100,000), 98% caused by PUUV, with Finland and Germany making up 69% of the total. From 2018 to 2025, Hungary recorded 51 lab-confirmed hantavirus infections, 20 of which were specifically linked to the PUUV. In Finland, between 560 and 3800 cases of NE are reported each year, though the actual number is believed to be nearly six times higher. PUUV is a spherical enveloped pathogen characterized by a segmented negative-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) genome. The PUUV possesses a tripartite genome: the L segment (~ 6.5 kb) encodes a ~ 2156-amino-acid L protein (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) with replicase, transcriptase, and endonuclease functions; the M segment (~ 3.7 kb) encodes a ~ 1148-amino-acid glycoprotein precursor that is co-translationally cleaved into Gn (70 kDa) and Gc (55 kDa); and the S segment (~ 1.8 kb) encodes a ~ 433-amino-acid nucleocapsid (N) protein. Gc is the protein that mediates fusion by the identification of a peptide of fusion, whereas Gn serves as a folding chaperone for Gc and controls the time of fusion; both are necessary for the virus to adhere as well as enter host cells. Gn and Gc form the principal antigenic surface of PUUV and are major targets of neutralizing antibodies, contributing to protective immunity and vaccine relevance. The N protein plays multiple roles in viral genome transport, replication, and assembly through its interactions with host cellular proteins, while also acting as a highly immunogenic viral component in both humans and animal models. The N protein is highly conserved among orthohantaviruses and elicits a strong early antibody response during acute infection, making it an important target for both diagnostic applications and vaccine development. Various vaccine platforms are available, each possessing distinct advantages and drawbacks. For example, live attenuated vaccines trigger strong, long-lasting immunity but can be risky for immunocompromised individuals due to possible reversion to virulence; inactivated vaccines are safer and more stable, though they usually require multiple doses; subunit vaccines use only key antigens, lowering the chance of side effects, but often need adjuvants and booster shots to achieve durable protection. Moreover, DNA vaccines offer rapid, stable, and cost-effective production with long-lasting immunity, but they often show weak immunogenicity in humans and face delivery challenges. In contrast, the key advantage of mRNA vaccines lies in their rapid design and production, enabling swift responses to emerging infections and pandemic threats without the need to culture live pathogens. In recognition of these advances, the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine honored Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman for their groundbreaking contributions to nucleoside engineering, a key innovation that enabled the successful development of mRNA vaccines against COVID-19. Recent developments in bioinformatics have improved biopharmaceutical design by enabling rapid prediction of protein features, structural modeling, and immunogenicity assessment. These computational approaches accelerate the identification and optimization of therapeutic candidates while reducing time and experimental costs; however, challenges related to prediction accuracy, biological complexity, and the need for experimental validation remain important considerations. Reverse vaccinology (RV) applies bioinformatics and immunoinformatics to screen microbial genomes for conserved, immunogenic epitopes, enabling faster, safer, and cost-effective vaccine development compared to traditional pathogen culturing, a slow and labor-intensive process. Vaccine development against PUUV infection has included inactivated whole-virus vaccines, recombinant subunit vaccines, virus-like particle (VLP)-based approaches, and DNA vaccines. Among these, inactivated and DNA vaccine candidates have demonstrated promising immunogenicity in preclinical studies. Currently, no vaccine has been authorized by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for PUUV infection. Several studies have suggested the potential of multi-epitope vaccine approaches using immunoinformatics-based strategies. Khan et al. developed a multi-epitope vaccine candidate against SARS-CoV-2 by integrating epitope prediction, antigenicity assessment, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response analysis, demonstrating the feasibility of computational vaccine design approaches. Similarly, Peele et al. designed a multi-epitope vaccine construct containing predicted B-cell and T-cell epitopes and evaluated its structural and immunological properties through computational analyses. These studies highlighted the potential of combining multiple immune targets within a single vaccine construct; however, their findings remained primarily dependent on computational predictions and required experimental validation to confirm immunogenicity and protective efficacy. However, despite these advances, several challenges remain in current multi-epitope vaccine development strategies. Computational vaccine designs are dependent on prediction algorithms, reference databases, structural modeling assumptions, and available biological information, which may influence the reliability of predicted vaccine candidates. In addition, variations in epitope selection criteria, antigen conservation analysis, population coverage evaluation, and structural validation approaches can affect the effectiveness of computational vaccine design. Recent studies have emphasized that although immunoinformatics approaches accelerate multi-epitope vaccine development, comprehensive experimental validation remains essential for confirming biological relevance and protective potential. Despite previous vaccine development efforts, including inactivated whole-virus vaccines, recombinant subunit vaccines, virus-like particle (VLP)-based approaches, and DNA vaccine candidates, no PUUV vaccine has currently received regulatory approval. An integrated mRNA multi-epitope vaccine strategy targeting conserved regions of both PUUV glycoproteins (Gn/Gc) and nucleocapsid protein remains insufficiently explored. A comprehensive framework combining conserved antigen identification, multi-epitope vaccine construction, structural evaluation, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response prediction for PUUV has not been extensively investigated. Therefore, this study aimed to design and evaluate the PV-GNProtecta vaccine candidate using an integrated immunoinformatics workflow involving conserved antigen identification, epitope prediction, structural modeling, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and immune response prediction. The findings provide computational insights into the potential characteristics of PV-GNProtecta while recognizing the necessity of experimental validation for future assessment. Materials and methods Acquisition and characterization of viral protein sequences The UniProt protein database (https://www.uniprot.org/; accessed on 15 July 2025) was used for obtaining amino acid sequences of the target proteins from PUUV of G (accession number: P41266) and N (accession numbers: P41270). The G and N proteins were selected due to their key roles in PUUV infection and immune recognition. The G protein mediates viral attachment and entry and is a major target of neutralizing antibodies, whereas the highly conserved N protein contributes to viral replication and induces strong immune responses. Compared with the intracellular RdRp/L protein, G and N provide more suitable targets for antibody and cellular immune responses. A comparative evaluation of these proteins is provided in Supplementary Table S14. Physicochemical and structural characterization of selected proteins The selected PUUV G and N proteins were characterized for signal peptide presence, transmembrane regions, and subcellular localization. Signal peptide prediction was performed using SignalP 6.0 (https://services.healthtech.dtu.dk/services/SignalP-6.0/; accessed on 15 September 2026) with the organism group selected as Eukarya and the default prediction model. Transmembrane topology was predicted using DeepTMHMM version 1.0.57 (accessed on 15 September 2026) using the default settings. Subcellular localization information was obtained from UniProt (https://www.uniprot.org/; accessed on 15 September 2026) based on available curated annotations. Analysis of multiple sequence alignment and evolutionary relationships To support RV analysis, the sequence is encoded using amino acid residue codes and preserved as a FASTA sequence file. The acquired sequences were subsequently utilized for multiple sequence alignment (MSA) through the Clustal Omega platform (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/jdispatcher/msa/clustalo; accessed on 05 August 2025). The Mega X tool (https://www.megasoftware.net/; accessed on 05 August 2025) was employed for phylogenetic analysis on both genomes. Prediction of epitopes for MHC I, MHC II, and linear B-cell interactions The MHC I epitopes from the G and N proteins were found using the Immune Epitope Database (IEDB) (http://tools.iedb.org/mhci/; accessed on 20 August 2025) software, with a percentile rank < 1.00 as the selection criterion. This tool is a sophisticated database comprising information on MHC molecules, T-cell and B-cell epitopes, antibodies, and MHC-binding ligands identified in humans and various animal taxonomic groups, including primates and rodents. A cutoff percentile rank of less than 1.00 was implemented for epitope selection, which suggests that the binding affinity was improved. Lower percentile rank values indicate stronger predicted peptide–MHC binding affinity. The IEDB (http://tools.iedb.org/mhcii/; accessed on 20 August 2025) was applied to forecast the MHC II epitopes inside the designated areas of these proteins, and peptides with percentile ranks < 1.00 were considered potential high-affinity binders and selected for further evaluation. Subsequently, the human allele reference sets were employed to predict CD8 + and CD4 + binding. The ABCpred tool (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/abcpred/; accessed on 25 August 2025) was used to estimate the continuous B-cell epitopes of the selected portions of these proteins. This tool provides epitope predictions by analyzing the sequence features of the target antigens. This program uses an affinity scale method based on a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to predict continuous B-cell epitopes. Additionally, the MHC-II epitopes underwent some additional analyses, including IL-10 (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/il10pred/; accessed on 25 September 2026), IFN-gamma (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/ifnepitope/predict.php; accessed on 25 September 2026), IL-2 (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/il2pred/; accessed on 25 September 2026) and IL-4 (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/il4pred/design.php; accessed on 25 September 2026) by using the respective servers. Linear B-cell epitopes were forecasted with ABCpred with a standard window length of 16 amino acids and a score cutoff of 0.51. Antigenicity was evaluated using the VaxiJen v2.0 (https://www.ddg-pharmfac.net/vaxijen/VaxiJen/VaxiJen.html; accessed on 28 August 2025) server under the viral protein model with the default threshold value of 0.4. Peptides with antigenicity scores ≥ 0.4 were considered probable antigens and retained for further analysis, whereas those scoring below this threshold were excluded. The threshold value of 0.4 was selected based on the default classification cutoff recommended for the VaxiJen viral model, which was established through performance evaluation of the prediction system. AllerTOP v2.1 (threshold: 0.5) (https://www.ddg-pharmfac.net/allertop_test/; accessed on 28 August 2025) and ToxinPred (threshold: 0.0) servers (https://webs.iiitd.edu.in/raghava/toxinpred/algo.php; accessed on 28 August 2025) were deployed in order to make predictions on allergenicity and toxicity, respectively. The allergenicity was evaluated utilizing AllerTOP v2.1 with the server's standard ACC/k-NN algorithm configurations. Also, toxicity prediction was performed using the ToxinPred server with the SVM (Swiss-Prot)-based prediction method, applying the default threshold value of 0.0 and a window length of 17 residues. Peptides were classified according to the server-generated SVM prediction score, and sequences predicted as toxic were excluded, whereas non-toxic peptides were retained for further analysis. All settings were preserved according to the server’s default configuration. The selected epitopes were not chosen based only on prediction scores; additional analyses, including antigenicity, safety assessment, sequence conservation, population coverage, and MHC interaction evaluation, were also considered to improve the reliability of epitope selection. Evaluation of population-level coverage The prevalence of HLA alleles varies across different geographies and ethnic communities. analysis.summary_en: Background: Puumala virus causes nephropathia epidemica, a zoonotic disease with renal complications and no approved vaccine. analysis_zh.limitations: 所有发现均基于体外计算分析;需进行实验验证以评估翻译效率、稳定性、表达和免疫原性。

papers.title: Framing the 2026 Global Hantavirus Outbreak in Nigerian Online Newspapers: Insights from Premium Times and Sahara Reporters
papers.abstract: Background: Emerging infectious diseases often attract significant media attention because of their potential impact on public health perceptions and preparedness. Despite the absence of confirmed cases in Nigeria, the 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak generated global public health concern because of increased international mobility and the potential risk of cross-border transmission. Objective: This study investigated how Premium Times and Sahara Reporters framed the 2026 global hantavirus outbreak, focusing on the frequency, presentation formats, prominence, and dominant frames of coverage. Method: The study employed a content analysis design. Using census approach, all hantavirus-related stories published by Premium Times and Sahara Reporters between 2 and 30 May 2026 were identified, yielding 29 stories for analysis. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, while Holsti’s (1969) formula was used to assess inter-coder reliability, yielding a reliability coefficient of 0.85. Results: Premium Times published 17 stories (58.6%), while Sahara Reporters published 12 stories (41.4%). Of the 29 stories, 24 (82.8%) were news stories, 19 (65.5%) received low prominence, and 10 (34.5%) adopted a health risk/awareness frame, followed by the prevention and safety measures frame (5 stories; 17.2%) and the attribution of responsibility frame (4 stories; 13.8%). Conclusion: Nigerian online newspapers reported the outbreak primarily as a public health risk but devoted limited attention and prominence to the issue, suggesting a predominantly reactive orientation in the newspapers' reporting of emerging health threats. Unique Contribution: This study contributes empirical evidence on Nigerian media framing of the 2026 global hantavirus outbreak and extends health communication scholarship on emerging zoonotic diseases. Key Recommendation: Nigerian online newspapers should adopt more sustained, prominent, explanatory, and interpretative reporting of emerging infectious diseases to strengthen public preparedness and risk communication.
authors: Valentine Okwudilichukwu Ezema, Sunday Uche Aja, Mercy Ifeyinwa Obichili, Joseph N. Chukwu, Chika Thonia Ezeali, Ijeoma Njideka Taiwo & Kelvin Chinemerem Nkwuda
papers.journal: International Journal of Sub-Saharan African Research

papers.title: Hantavirus Outbreak on MV Hondius Cruise Ship: India’s Port Health Preparedness – A One Health Perspective
papers.abstract: Abstract The MV Hondius outbreak, reported in May 2026, is among the first large multinational hantavirus clusters linked to cruise ship travel. By July 2, 2026, when the outbreak was declared over, 13 cases (12 laboratory-confirmed and one probable) and three deaths had been reported, with contact tracing involving 33 countries and territories; no confirmed cases were reported in India. The identified Andes virus strain is notable for limited person-to-person transmission. This viewpoint is an interpretation of the outbreak using publicly available reports, scientific literature, and official communications from health agencies within a One Health framework, focusing on implications for India’s port health preparedness. The outbreak highlights how ecological exposure, international mobility, and a confined maritime environment can facilitate disease spread. India’s port health infrastructure includes pre-arrival vessel risk assessment, passenger thermal scanning, and contingency plans aligned with the International Health Regulations (IHR) 2005. Although hantavirus strains identified in India are not associated with person-to-person transmission, existing seroprevalence data support the need for continued surveillance. Strengthening a One Health approach integrating human, animal, and environmental surveillance is essential for future maritime outbreak preparedness. Trained port health personnel, improved diagnostics, and effective public communication remain essential.

source_records.abstract: Abstract The MV Hondius outbreak, reported in May 2026, is among the first large multinational hantavirus clusters linked to cruise ship travel. By July 2, 2026, when the outbreak was declared over, 13 cases (12 laboratory-confirmed and one probable) and three deaths had been reported, with contact tracing involving 33 countries and territories; no confirmed cases were reported in India. The identified Andes virus strain is notable for limited person-to-person transmission. This viewpoint is an interpretation of the outbreak using publicly available reports, scientific literature, and official communications from health agencies within a One Health framework, focusing on implications for India’s port health preparedness. The outbreak highlights how ecological exposure, international mobility, and a confined maritime environment can facilitate disease spread. India’s port health infrastructure includes pre-arrival vessel risk assessment, passenger thermal scanning, and contingency plans aligned with the International Health Regulations (IHR) 2005. Although hantavirus strains identified in India are not associated with person-to-person transmission, existing seroprevalence data support the need for continued surveillance. Strengthening a One Health approach integrating human, animal, and environmental surveillance is essential for future maritime outbreak preparedness. Trained port health personnel, improved diagnostics, and effective public communication remain essential.

papers.title: Human febrile illness associated with Yanggou tick virus: Clinical characteristics and epidemiological links to rodents.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: We identified Yanggou tick virus (YGTV), a segmented flavivirus previously unrecognized as a human pathogen, in a patient presenting with fever and headache. This study aims to characterize the epidemiology and clinical manifestations of YGTV infection in patients with fever of unknown origin (FUO). METHODS: We conducted a surveillance study at the First Hospital of Jilin University (2020-2025) involving 1,011 patients with FUO. Concurrently, ticks and rodents in the vicinity of the patients' residences and workplaces were collected for viral detection. YGTV infection was confirmed via PCR assays. Positive samples were used for viral isolation, genome amplification, and phylogenetic characterization. An Apodemus agrarius challenge model was established to evaluate viral persistence and shedding. RESULTS: Of the 30 confirmed cases of YGTV infection, 10 were co-diagnosed with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). The patients showed no clear seasonality or geographic bias. Notably, rodent contact (43.3%) was a more frequent risk factor than tick bites (6.7%). While clinical presentations were non-specific, nearly 50% of the patients presented with gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms. YGTV was isolated from patients, ticks, and A. agrarius (the latter often co-infected with Hantaan virus). Animal models confirmed persistent splenic infection and viral shedding via oral and fecal routes. CONCLUSION: Our findings establish YGTV as an underdiagnosed cause of human febrile illness, underscoring the transmission risks posed by tick vectors and rodent reservoirs. These results highlight the urgent need for enhanced clinical surveillance and diagnostic screening among patients presenting with FUO, particularly in regions where the virus is endemic.

analysis.summary_en: Background: YGTV, a segmented flavivirus previously unrecognized as a human pathogen, was identified in a patient with fever and headache. Methods: A surveillance study (2020‑2025) at First Hospital of Jilin University enrolled 1,011 FUO patients; ticks and rodents near patients’ homes/workplaces were collected; infection was confirmed by PCR, followed by viral isolation, genome sequencing, phylogenetics, and an Apodemus agrarius challenge model to assess persistence and shedding. papers.title_zh: 与羊沟蜱病毒相关的人类发热疾病:临床特征及与啮齿动物的流行病学关联

analysis_zh.background: 目标:Yanggou蜱病毒(YGTV),一种先前未被认定为人类致病的分段黄病毒,在一例发热头痛患者中被发现。
analysis_zh.methods: 在吉林大学第一医院开展的监测研究(2020‐2025)中,纳入了1,011例发热未明原因(FUO)患者;采集患者居住/工作地点附近的蜱和啮齿动物;通过PCR确认YGTV感染;对阳性样本进行病毒分离、基因组扩增和系统发育分析;使用田野鼠(Apodemus agrarius)挑战模型评估病毒的持续感染和排泄。
analysis_zh.results: 共确认30例YGTV感染病例,其中10例合并诊断为肾综合征出血热;病例未表现出明显的季节性或地域偏好;啮齿动物接触率为43.3%,高于蜱叮咬率6.7%;约50%的患者出现胃肠或神经系统症状;YGTV已从患者、蜱和田野鼠(A. agrarius)中分离(常与汉滩病毒共感染);动物模型显示脾脏持续感染并通过口腔/粪便排泄。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究结果确认YGTV是人类发热疾病的潜在漏诊病因,强调蜱和啮齿动物储存宿主的传播风险,并指出在流行地区需加强临床监测和诊断筛查。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅有摘要数据;未报告详细方法、媒介样本量及统计分析。

papers.title: Fractional optimal control of hantavirus transmission between rodents and humans
papers.abstract: This paper studies a fractional optimal control problem for a hantavirus transmission model involving interactions between rodent reservoirs and human populations. The model is formulated through a modified SIR–SIR structure, where both humans and rodents are divided into susceptible, infected, and recovered classes. The classical integer-order model is extended by using the Caputo fractional derivative, which captures memory and hereditary effects in the disease dynamics. Three time-dependent control variables are introduced: rodent culling, environmental sanitation, and treatment of infected humans. Positivity, boundedness, existence, and uniqueness of solutions are established to guarantee the biological and mathematical validity of the model. An optimal control problem is then formulated to minimize infected humans, infected rodents, and the costs of intervention. Necessary optimality conditions are derived using Pontryagin’s maximum principle for fractional systems. The adjoint equations, transversality conditions, and explicit characterization of the optimal controls are obtained. A numerical scheme based on the fractional Adams–Bashforth–Moulton predictor–corrector method combined with the forward–backward sweep algorithm is implemented. Several numerical scenarios are investigated, including no control, single-control strategies, and combined optimal controls. The simulations show that the combined strategy gives the strongest reduction in both infected humans and infected rodents. The results illustrate how memory-dependent dynamics can alter the predicted transmission trajectories and optimal intervention profiles. However, empirical calibration and validation using compatible human and rodent surveillance data are required before the model can be used for outbreak-specific prediction.

Keywords Hantavirus transmission, Fractional optimal control, Caputo derivative, Pontryagin maximum principle, Fractional epidemic systems, Forward–backward sweep method Hantavirus infection is a serious zoonotic disease transmitted mainly through infected rodents and contaminated environmental materials such as urine, saliva, and feces1–3. The disease represents an important global public health challenge because of its high mortality rates, rapid respiratory complications, and increasing geographical spread4–6. Several strains of hantaviruses have been identified worldwide, including strains responsible for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome7–9. Human infection generally occurs through inhalation of aerosolized particles from infected rodents, although evidence of human-to- human transmission has also been reported in specific outbreaks10 (Fig. 1). Rodents are considered the principal reservoirs of hantaviruses12,13. Long-term epidemiological studies confirmed that environmental conditions, climate fluctuations, rodent migration, and habitat changes play significant roles in the persistence and transmission of hantavirus infection14–18. In Asia and South America, several investigations revealed increasing prevalence rates associated with ecological changes and urbanization5,9,19. In Indonesia, hantavirus infections have attracted increasing scientific interest due to the existence of infected rodent reservoirs in several provinces20–22. Mathematical modeling has become an essential tool for understanding the spread and control of infectious diseases23–26. Classical epidemic models based on ordinary differential equations have been successfully applied to many zoonotic diseases27,28. Several mathematical models for hantavirus transmission have been developed in the literature. Abramson and Kenkre studied spatial and spatiotemporal patterns in hantavirus spread14,15. Allen et al. proposed deterministic and ecological models describing rodent-host interactions and environmental variability29–31. Wesley et al. analyzed direct and indirect transmission mechanisms in rodent Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:31685 2 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-72549-0 www.nature.com/scientificreports populations32. Additional modeling investigations involving ecological risk mapping, stochastic fluctuations, and environmental effects were developed in33–35. Although classical integer-order models provide useful qualitative insights, they often fail to capture memory and hereditary effects observed in biological systems. Many infectious diseases exhibit nonlocal temporal dynamics in which the future state depends not only on the present state but also on the history of the system. Fractional calculus provides a powerful mathematical framework for incorporating these memory effects into epidemiological models36–38. Fractional-order epidemic models have shown improved accuracy in describing long-memory biological processes and nonlinear transmission dynamics39. Biological justification for the Caputo derivative The use of the Caputo fractional derivative is motivated by biological and epidemiological processes that depend on accumulated history rather than only on the current state. Hantavirus risk is influenced by prior rodent abundance, repeated or prolonged contact with contaminated excreta, persistence of infectious material in the environment, delayed effects of habitat and climate variation, and time-distributed host recovery and immune responses. These mechanisms introduce temporal dependence that may not be represented adequately by a local first-order derivative. The Caputo operator describes such effects through a power-law memory kernel, so recent and earlier epidemic states contribute with different weights to the present rate of change. It is also suitable for population models because it permits conventional initial conditions expressed directly through the initial compartment sizes. The fractional order inline-eq-IEq1 is therefore interpreted as a phenomenological memory parameter. The value in l ine-eq-IEq2 recovers the memory-free classical model, whereas i n line-eq-IEq3 αne-eq-IEq3 represents nonlocal temporal dependence of increasing strength. Its epidemiological relevance should be assessed through sensitivity analysis, parameter estimation, and comparison with observed data. Recently, fractional optimal control theory has received considerable attention in mathematical biology and engineering40. The combination of fractional dynamics and optimal control allows the construction of realistic control strategies that account for memory-dependent disease behavior while minimizing intervention costs. Several important developments in fractional optimal control systems were established in41–43. Applications involving epidemic systems, cancer dynamics, and quantum systems, dark mater in cosmological models demonstrated the efficiency of fractional optimal control formulations44–48. Despite the large number of studies devoted to hantavirus transmission dynamics, very few works considered fractional-order optimal control formulations for hantavirus systems. Most existing models are formulated using classical differential equations without incorporating memory effects or optimal intervention strategies. Moreover, the combined effects of rodent reduction, environmental sanitation, and treatment controls within a fractional-order framework remain insufficiently investigated. Recent studies have demonstrated the value of combining fractional-order operators with biologically structured transmission mechanisms, parameter estimation, threshold analysis, and optimal control. Caputo fractional models have been developed for foot-and-mouth disease with environmental transmission and intervention strategies, as well as for norovirus transmission with vaccination and an environmental reservoir49,50. These studies illustrate how memory effects and environmental persistence can be incorporated into infectious- disease systems. Fractional rabies models have also provided several relevant methodological developments. Caputo models calibrated through Markov chain Monte Carlo methods have been used to estimate uncertain transmission parameters and evaluate public-health interventions51. Related investigations have considered dog vaccination within a Caputo framework52, and rabies dynamics formulated with the Atangana–Baleanu–Caputo derivative and MCMC parameter estimation53. Comparative analyses of singular and nonsingular fractional operators have further clarified how alternative memory kernels influence epidemic trajectories54. Moreover, fractional optimal control and cost-effectiveness analysis have been applied to rabies interventions, demonstrating the practical importance of combining memory-dependent dynamics with intervention design55. Several recent works have also strengthened the theoretical foundation of fractional epidemic modeling. In a related study, a fractional epidemiological model incorporating vaccination and quarantine compartments was analyzed with respect to well-posedness, threshold behavior, stability, and optimal intervention56. Viral particles released from rodent excreta become aerosolized and may be inhaled by humans, leading to respiratory infection. The inset illustrates microscopic viral particles associated with the transmission pathway11. Fractional optimal control has also been applied to other nonlinear biological systems, including cancer–obesity dynamics, illustrating the broader applicability of Pontryagin-type methods in memory-dependent models58. Recent data-informed studies further highlight the importance of model calibration and uncertainty assessment. A fractional trachoma model calibrated with epidemiological data from Cameroon demonstrated how the fractional order can be estimated and interpreted using real observations59. Although the latter concerns plant disease, its mathematical framework remains relevant to the analysis of nonlinear disease systems. Taken together, these contributions support the use of fractional calculus, sensitivity analysis, and data-based estimation in infectious-disease modeling. The present work differs by focusing on hantavirus transmission between a persistent rodent reservoir and dead-end human hosts, while simultaneously incorporating rodent culling, environmental sanitation, and treatment of infected humans within a unified fractional optimal control framework. Motivated by these observations, this paper develops a new fractional optimal control model for hantavirus transmission dynamics between rodents and humans. The proposed model extends the classical hantavirus transmission framework by introducing Caputo fractional derivatives to capture hereditary effects in the disease dynamics. Three control variables are incorporated representing rodent elimination, environmental sanitation, and treatment efforts for infected individuals. Novelty of the study. The novelty of the present study lies in extending existing hantavirus transmission models in three connected directions. First, unlike classical integer-order models that describe rodent–human transmission without temporal memory, the proposed system uses the Caputo fractional derivative to represent hereditary and history-dependent effects. Second, the model integrates three intervention mechanisms— rodent culling, environmental sanitation, and treatment of infected humans—within a single optimal control framework. Third, the study provides a complete analytical and computational treatment, including positivity, boundedness, existence and uniqueness, equilibrium and stability analysis, the fractional Pontryagin optimality system, and a comparative assessment of no-control, single-control, and combined-control strategies. To the best of our knowledge, this combination has not been developed previously for hantavirus transmission between rodents and humans. Aim of the study. The main aim of this study is to develop and analyze a fractional optimal control model for hantavirus transmission between rodents and humans. The proposed model extends the classical SIR–SIR hantavirus framework by replacing the integer-order time derivative with the Caputo fractional derivative. This extension allows the model to account for memory effects, hereditary behavior, and the influence of past infection history on the current disease dynamics. The study also aims to design effective intervention strategies that reduce the number of infected humans and infected rodents while minimizing the cost of control implementation. To achieve this goal, three time- dependent controls are introduced: rodent culling, environmental sanitation, and treatment of infected humans. The mathematical analysis focuses on positivity, boundedness, existence, uniqueness, equilibrium behavior, and stability of the fractional model. In addition, Pontryagin’s maximum principle is used to derive the necessary optimality conditions, including the adjoint system and explicit control characterizations. A further aim is to investigate the numerical behavior of the model under different control scenarios and different fractional orders. The numerical simulations compare the uncontrolled case, single-control strategies, and combined optimal controls. This comparison helps identify the most effective strategy for reducing hantavirus transmission and highlights the role of the fractional-order parameter in producing smoother and more realistic epidemic trajectories. Innovation and applications The present study introduces a fractional optimal control framework for hantavirus transmission between rodents and humans. The innovation of the work lies in combining fractional-order epidemic modeling, rodent– human transmission dynamics, and optimal control theory in one unified mathematical structure. Unlike classical integer-order models, the proposed system uses the Caputo fractional derivative to describe memory-dependent disease evolution. This allows the model to account for past environmental exposure, previous rodent density, and accumulated contamination effects. Such effects are important in hantavirus transmission because the infection process depends not only on the current number of infected rodents but also on past ecological and epidemiological conditions. The main innovations of this work are summarized as follows: • A fractional SIR–SIR hantavirus transmission model is formulated for both human and rodent populations. • The Caputo fractional derivative is used to incorporate memory and hereditary effects into the epidemic dynamics. • Three realistic control strategies are introduced: rodent culling, sanitation, and treatment. • The model combines reservoir control, exposure reduction, and clinical intervention in a single optimal con­ trol problem. • Positivity, boundedness, existence, and uniqueness of solutions are established. • The basic reproduction number is analyzed to describe the persistence or elimination of infection. • Pontryagin’s maximum principle is applied to derive the adjoint system and the explicit characterization of optimal controls. • A fractional Adams–Bashforth–Moulton scheme with a forward–backward sweep method is used to solve the optimality system. Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:31685 4 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-72549-0 www.nature.com/scientificreports • Several numerical scenarios are compared to identify the most effective control policy. • The influence of the fractional-order parameter inline-eq-IEq4 is studied to show the role of memory effects in disease progression. The proposed model has several practical applications. It can help public health authorities evaluate different intervention strategies before implementation. It can also support decision-making in areas where hantavirus infection is linked to rodent density, environmental contamination, and limited healthcare resources. The rodent culling control inline-eq-IEq5 can guide policies related to trapping, poisoning, habitat destruction, and rodent population monitoring. The sanitation control inline-eq-IEq6 can support cleaning campaigns, safe waste removal, protection of food storage areas, and reduction of human exposure to rodent excreta. The treatment control inline-eq-IEq7 can help assess the impact of clinical care, hospitalization, and recovery-support programs. The numerical results show that combined optimal controls provide the strongest reduction in infected humans and infected rodents. This suggests that hantavirus control should not depend on a single intervention. A practical control program should combine reservoir reduction, environmental sanitation, and clinical treatment. From a mathematical viewpoint, the study contributes to fractional epidemic control theory by extending optimal control methods to a zoonotic disease model with two interacting populations. From an epidemiological viewpoint, it provides a flexible tool for studying hantavirus transmission under memory-dependent dynamics. papers.title_zh: 分数阶最优控制 汉坦病毒 在啮齿动物与人类之间的传播

analysis_zh.background: 本研究针对 汉坦病毒 在啮齿动物与人类之间的传播进行探讨,该人畜共患病致死率高且地理分布正在扩大。
analysis_zh.methods: 构建了一个带 Caputo 导数的分数阶 SIR–SIR 模型,纳入啮齿动物扑杀、环境卫生和人类治疗作为时间依赖的控制措施;证明了模型的存在性、唯一性和有界性,并基于 Pontryagin 原理提出并求解了最优控制问题,采用分数阶 Adams–Bashforth–Moulton 预测-校正方案。
analysis_zh.results: 对无控制、单一控制和组合控制情景进行数值模拟,结果表明组合策略在降低感染人群和啮齿动物数量方面效果最显著,展示了记忆效应如何改变传播轨迹。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究展示了分数阶动力学如何为 汉坦病毒 的最优干预方案提供依据,强调在针对特定暴发应用前需进行实证校准。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：本研究针对 汉坦病毒 在啮齿动物与人类之间的传播进行探讨,该人畜共患病致死率高且地理分布正在扩大。 方法：构建了一个带 Caputo 导数的分数阶 SIR–SIR 模型,纳入啮齿动物扑杀、环境卫生和人类治疗作为时间依赖的控制措施;证明了模型的存在性… 结果：对无控制、单一控制和组合控制情景进行数值模拟,结果表明组合策略在降低感染人群和啮齿动物数量方面效果最显著,展示了记忆效应如何改变传播轨迹。 贡献：本研究展示了分数阶动力学如何为 汉坦病毒 的最优干预方案提供依据,强调在针对特定暴发应用前需进行实证校准。 局限：模型缺乏基于监测数据的实证校准和验证,研究仅限于理论模拟,未报告现场数据。

papers.title: Current State of Diagnostics of Hemorrhagic Fevers Caused by Viruses of the Genera Orthonairovirus, Phlebovirus, Orthohantavirus and Orthoflavivirus, Using the LAMP Method
papers.abstract: The work is an overview of the data on application of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) for the diagnosis of viral hemorrhagic fevers caused by pathogens belonging to the second pathogenicity group. The first part of the review provides a brief characterization of the main viral agents of hemorrhagic fevers from the families Nairoviridae, Phenuiviridae, Hantaviridae, and Flaviviridae. Special attention is given to the epidemiological significance of these pathogens and the challenges associated with their timely laboratory identification. The aim of the study was to analyze and systematize the data available in the literature sources on the use of LAMP as an alternative to polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for diagnosing hemorrhagic fevers caused by these agents. The review considers the principal methods for registering LAMP results, including the turbidimetric method, immunochromatographic assays, the use of fluorescent dyes, metal-based indicators and pH-sensitive dyes. A comparative analysis of the analytical characteristics of existing LAMP reagent kits for each of the described agents is also presented. It is noted that there are currently no registered and widely available commercial LAMP reagent kits for detecting the genetic markers of these viruses. This underscores the need for further research, since the implementation of rapid and reliable diagnostic methods suitable for field use is a prerequisite for effective epidemic control measures. Therefore, the development of appropriate reagent kits based on the LAMP method represents a promising objective.

Чуб1 Современное состояние диагностики геморрагических лихорадок, вызываемых вирусами родов Orthonairovirus, Phlebovirus, Orthohantavirus и Orthoflavivirus методом LAMP 1Государственный научный центр вирусологии и биотехнологии «Вектор», р.п. Кольцово, Российская Федерация; 2Новосибирский национальный исследовательский государственный университет, Новосибирск, Российская Федерация Представлен обзор данных о применении метода петлевой изотермической амплификации (loop mediated isothermal amplification, LAMP) для диагностики вирусных геморрагических лихорадок, вызываемых возбудите­ лями, относящимися к II группе патогенности. Дана краткая характеристика основных вирусных возбудителей геморрагических лихорадок из семейств Nairoviridae, Phenuiviridae, Hantaviridae и Flaviviridae. Особое внимание уделено эпидемиологической значимости данных патогенов и сложности их своевременной лабораторной иден­ тификации. Основная цель работы заключалась в анализе и систематизации имеющихся в литературе данных об использовании метода LAMP как альтернативы ПЦР для диагностики геморрагических лихорадок, вызываемых данными возбудителями. Рассмотрены основные методы детекции результатов LAMP, включая турбидиметри­ ческий метод, иммунохроматографический анализ, использование флуоресцентных красителей, металлоинди­ каторов и pH-чувствительных красителей. Проведен сравнительный анализ аналитических характеристик раз­ работанных наборов реагентов для LAMP-диагностики каждого из рассматриваемых возбудителей. Отмечается, что в настоящее время не существует зарегистрированных и широкодоступных коммерческих LAMP-наборов реагентов для выявления генетических маркеров данных вирусов. Это актуализирует необходимость дальнейших исследований, так как внедрение быстрых и надежных методов диагностики, пригодных для использования в полевых условиях, является необходимым условием эффективных противоэпидемических мероприятий. Таким образом, разработка соответствующих наборов реагентов на основе метода LAMP представляет собой перспек­ тивную задачу. Ключевые слова: геморрагическая лихорадка, изотермическая амплификация, LAMP, диагностика. Корреспондирующий автор: Беличенко Ксения Руслановна, e-mail: ksenbelichen@gmail.com. Такие серьезные заболевания часто вызывают вирусы I и II группы патогенности, со­ гласно российской классификации патогенных для человека микроорганизмов. К вирусам II группы патогенности, вызывающим ВГЛ у людей, относят­ ся некоторые представители родов Orthonairovirus (сем. Nairoviridae), Phlebovirus (сем. Phenuiviridae), Orthohantavirus (сем. Hantaviridae) и Orthoflavivirus (сем. Flaviviridae) (табл. 1). Эти вирусы, способные вызывать вспышки ВГЛ с высокой летальностью, представляют большой ин­ терес для здравоохранения. В роде Orthonairovirus CCHFV способен вы­ зывать Крымскую-Конго геморрагическую ли­ хорадку, переносимую клещами рода Hyalomma. Зарегистрированы случаи заболевания данной ли­ хорадкой в Азии, Юго-Западной и Юго-Восточной Европе и Африке [1]. Инфекция у человека может протекать как в легкой форме, без специфических клинических симптомов, так и в тяжелой форме, до­ стигая уровня летальности 40 % [2]. Геном CCHFV состоит из трех сегментов РНК с отрицательной по­ лярностью: S (1,7 кб), M (5,4 кб) и L (12,1 кб). Вирус обладает большим генетическим разнообразием и демонстрирует высокую изменчивость во всех трех сегментах. Так, разница в нуклеотидной последо­ вательности для S-сегмента составляет 20 %, для M – 31 %, для L – 22 % [3, 4]. В аминокислотной последовательности S- и L-сегменты также более консервативны (95 %), чем M-сегмент (до 75 %) [4]. Выделяется 7 генетических линий, основанных на S-сегменте: Африка 1–3, Азия 1, 2 и Европа 1, 2. RVFV из рода Phlebovirus является возбудите­ лем одноименного зоонозного заболевания, пере­ носимого комарами родов Aedes, Culex, Anopheles, Eretmapoites, Mansonia. Лихорадка долины Рифт была зарегистрирована в большинстве африканских стран, Саудовской Аравии и Йемене. Заболевание может протекать в тяжелой форме с ретинитом, ге­ патитом и энцефалитом, у 1 % пациентов развива­ ется геморрагическая лихорадка, уровень летально­ сти достигает 50 % [5, 6]. Геном вируса состоит из двух сегментов РНК с отрицательной полярностью M (3,9 кб) и L (6,4 кб) и одного сегмента амбисенс­ ной РНК – S (1,7 кб) [7]. Геном RVFV достаточно консервативен, лишь М-сегмент имеет небольшие различия в нуклеотидной (5 %) и аминокислотной (2 %) последовательности [8]. Хантавирусы (род Orthohantavirus) способны вызывать у человека геморрагическую лихорадку с почечным синдромом (ГЛПС) и хантавирусный пульмональный синдром (ХПС), передаваемые грызунами. Случаи заболевания ГЛПС, вызванные пре­имущественно вирусом Хантаан (HTNV), за­ регистрированы в Европе, России и Азии [9]. В за­ висимости от возбудителя уровень летальности до­ стигает 15 %.
